title: Вторая стычка с отцом Насти и соцсеть  (Second Clash with Nastya's Father and Social Media)

segments.t: Visiting Nastya's father at his meatpacking plant to apologize for their last fight, Kostya gets goaded into showing how he threw the punch and accidentally breaks her father's nose all over again. Back at the restaurant, Max tells Chef Barinov that he registered him on the social network and added Elena.
Ну, бей давай, я тебе покажу.
Я тебе сейчас в фарш добавлю.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
'I am going to lose this bet.' Barinov holds a wry style without hesitation, anchoring the Russian line on "prosporyu" ("lose a bet") and "ya" ("I") without extra filler.
'Well, what did you want?' Max wonders boldly beside Barinov, building the phrase around "khotel" ("wanted") and "nu" ("oh, come on") for a crisp, natural delivery.

'You only beat me last time because you caught me off guard.' Barinov projects a playful footing at this moment, linking "vrasplokh" ("off guard, unawares"), "stal" ("to become"), and "pobil" ("beat up") in one brisk exchange.
'Well, you could put it that way.' Max conveys a steady rhythm in the conversation, leaning on "mozhno" ("may, can") before closing the thought with "skazat" ("tell").
'Wait, I did not quite get that.' Barinov brings an unhurried tempo beside Max, putting "ponyal" ("understood") alongside "ya" ("I") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Ну, бей давай, я тебе покажу.
'Come on, throw a punch, I will show you how to block it.' Max shows a lively bearing with Barinov, joining "bey" ("to beat, to hit") to "davay" ("let's") so every word pulls its weight.
'Oh, well in that case, here I go.' Barinov holds a pointed angle across the room, building the phrase around "togda" ("back then") and "budu" ("will be") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'I am so sorry, please forgive me.' Max strikes a clear approach at this moment, pairing "izvinite" ("sorry, excuse me") with "pozhaluysta" ("please") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'I think he just broke your nose.' Barinov establishes a calm tempo in front of Max, putting "kazhetsya" ("it seems, I think") alongside "slomal" ("broke") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Chef, good afternoon.' Max holds a resolute note as they talk, joining "dobryy" ("good") to "den" ("day") so every word pulls its weight.
'What I wanted to tell you is...' Barinov challenges sharply to Max here, weaving "skazat" ("tell") together with "khotel" ("wanted") just the way native speakers do.
'Did you add me as a friend?' Max inquires pointedly toward Barinov here, pairing "druzya" ("friends") with "dobavte" ("to add, to supplement") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Я тебе сейчас в фарш добавлю.
'I am about to add you to the meat grinder.' Barinov shares an easygoing note at once, anchoring the Russian line on "seychas" ("now") and "farsh" ("minced") without extra filler.
Ну, бей давай, я тебе покажу.
Я тебе сейчас в фарш добавлю.

That wraps up this scene as kostya visits Nastya's father at his sausage factory to apologize, only to accidentally break his nose in a sparring demonstration, while Max registers Barinov online. Until next time!
